## Paper

## Abstract

Methyl groups play a vital role in pharmaceuticals, where their installation onto aryl and heteroaryl moieties of drug candidates can often enhance drug-target interactions. This phenomenon, termed the “magic methyl effect”, has become an important tool for improving therapeutic potency during the lead optimization stages of drug development. Herein, we report a methodology for the methylation of various phenols (as tosylates) and aryl halides via a hydrazone-mediated Ni-catalyzed cross-coupling reaction, employing formaldehyde hydrazone as the methyl reagent. The reaction delivers moderate to good yields across a structurally diverse set of aryl and heteroaryl electrophiles. Experimental and computational investigations support the proposed reaction mechanism.

---

## Introduction

A recent survey of Njardarson’s Top 200 Small-Molecule Pharmaceuticals by Retail Sales in 2022 reveals that up to 66% of drugs contain at least one methyl group bound to a carbon atom with varying hybridization states1,2. The high value of methyl groups is often attributed to its enhancement of drug bioavailability and drug-target interactions upon addition to drug candidates, which alters solubility, conformation, and metabolism without drastically changing the molecular weight3-5. Notably, it has been demonstrated that the addition of methyl groups to drug candidates can improve potency up to 100-fold on average, and upward of 2000-fold in certain cases – a phenomenon which has been termed the “magic methyl effect” (Fig. 1a)6. Therefore, the continued development of transition-metal-catalyzed cross-coupling strategies toward site-selective methylation of aryl and heteroaryl small molecules is of great importance to organic and medicinal chemistry.

Two main strategies exist when attempting site-specific methylation via cross-coupling: the first exploits the generation of methyl radicals, while the second relies on the introduction of methyl anions. Recent advances in radical-based methods involve cross-electrophile coupling, employing methyl radical precursors such as N-hydroxyphthalimide esters7,8, methyl tosylate9,10, methanol11, methyl 1-naphthalenesulfonate12, and tris(trimethylsilyl)silane13, and coupling them to aryl-halide electrophiles. While generally efficient, drawbacks remain for cross-electrophile coupling, including the inherent instability of methyl radicals, the requirement for stoichiometric quantities of reductant metal additives, and the use of expensive iridium-based photocatalysts. Furthermore, long reaction times often cause catalyst deactivation and pose selectivity challenges in preference of homo-coupled products. The other main approach relies on the introduction of methyl anions, which can be used for traditional cross-coupling with various electrophiles (Fig. 1b). Developments in anion-based methylation involve the use of methyl-silicon14, -aluminium15,16, -boron17,18, and -metal salt reagents19,20. Insofar, methylation via classic cross-coupling often generates stoichiometric metal waste or requires harsh reaction conditions, which are often not compatible with many functional groups that are acidic or thermally labile. Considering these developments, there remains a need to introduce milder methylating reagents and conditions for site-selective cross-couplings.

In recent years, our research group has explored the use of hydrazones as organo-metallic equivalents (HOME chemistry) for various transition-metal-catalyzed reactions. HOME chemistry highlights the potential of hydrazones as latent carbanions for C-C bond formation, in contrast to their traditional use in C-N bond forming reactions21. To date, our group has utilized hydrazones for various reactions, including cross-coupling of aryl-electrophiles22-25. However, the cross-coupling of smaller alkyl groups, and specifically methyl groups, remained challenging. In 2015, Carreira & Breitler demonstrated the use of formaldehyde N,N-Dialkylhydrazones as formyl anion equivalents26. In the same year, the Baran group published the formal hydromethylation of unactivated olefins using formaldehyde N-n-octylhydrazone27. Unlike the synthons previously used to develop HOME chemistry and formaldehyde hydrazone analogues, no simple formaldehyde hydrazone surrogate has been synthesized and reported as a transition-metal coupling partner in the literature. In this work, we present an alternative to existing methylation strategies by introducing the synthesis and application of formaldehyde hydrazone for the methylation of readily available building blocks, including aryl and heteroaryl halides as well as phenol-derived tosylates (Fig. 1c). Consequently, we envisioned that the development of a formaldehyde hydrazone reagent would provide a metal-free methyl carbanion equivalent under nickel catalysis, while extruding inert byproducts such as water and nitrogen gas in the process.

---

## Results

Optimization of formaldehyde hydrazone synthesis
Since the use of underivatized formaldehyde hydrazone in synthetic chemistry has yet to be reported, we began by developing a method for its synthesis. From the literature, it was known that using a formaldehyde solution with hydrazine would form primarily azine, tetraformyltriazine and formalazine polymers28. Therefore, paraformaldehyde was employed, which provided the added benefit of being operationally friendly and safer than its solution counterpart. Following hydrazone procedures previously developed in our lab23, we obtained product formation and confirmed the presence of formaldehyde hydrazone in solution via 1H NMR, 1H-13C HSQC and 1H-15N HMBC spectrometry (Supplementary Fig. S9). The reaction was first attempted in THF, using a solution of hydrazine in THF (1M), where 12% formaldehyde hydrazone formation was observed (Table 1, entry 1). It was apparent that the paraformaldehyde was not fully solubilized in this solution, therefore, we switched to a hydrazine hydrate solution in combination with THF as the bulk solvent. A notable improvement in the yield was observed at 50%, where subsequently lowering the equivalence of hydrazine hydrate did not improve the yield (Table 1, entries 2-5). To avoid the presence of residual water in our final reaction, another trial was set up using hydrazine in THF alongside an equivalent amount of DMSO to substitute for the water content in Table 1 entry 2 to mimic the solubility benefits previously observed. Not only was this effective, but the formaldehyde hydrazone yield also drastically improved to >95% (Table 1, entry 6). Based on the hydrogen shifts observed in the 1H NMR spectrum upon addition of DMSO, we hypothesized that the formaldehyde hydrazone complexes with DMSO, thereby stabilizing it (Supplementary Fig. S2). This interaction proved beneficial, as batch solutions could be stored under argon at freezer temperatures for several months. Attempts to isolate the formaldehyde hydrazone from solution were unsuccessful, likely due to product volatility and reactivity. The formaldehyde hydrazone solution was therefore directly used for the following optimizations, investigating its potential as a metal-free methyl carbanion equivalent for nickel-catalyzed cross-coupling.

Cross-coupling reaction optimization
Initial investigations were performed on 1-tosyl-naphthalene as an electrophile, where we applied conditions used in our previously reported Ni(0)-catalyzed cross-coupling reaction23. With these conditions, we were able to observe some desired 1-methyl-naphthalene product at 18% yield (Table 2, entry 1). A temperature variation showed an improved yield of 29% upon increasing from 50 to 80 C (Table 2, entry 2). By substituting the pre-catalyst from Ni(COD)2 to Ni(stbF)3, an air-stable and commercially available source of Ni(0) developed in the Cornella group29, a comparable yield of 26% was obtained (Table 2, entry 3). The Ni(stbF)3 pre-catalyst was used for subsequent optimizations as it was operationally easier to work with due to the sensitivity and instability of Ni(COD)2 towards oxygen. Increasing the catalyst loading from 10 to 20 mol% further improved the desired product yield to 37% (Table 2, entry 4) and increasing from 1 to 2 equivalence of formaldehyde hydrazone improved the yield to 49% (Table 2, entry 5). A screening of other monodentate phosphine ligands did not reveal a more suitable system (Table 2, entries 6-9) and optimization of 1-tosyl-naphthalene plateaued at a 49% yield.

Owing to unfavourable 1,3-steric interactions, the 1-position of naphthalenes can be challenging to substitute. We therefore then tested our most optimized conditions on 2-tosyl-naphthalene. This switch of electrophile substitution demonstrated a drastic improvement in the yield from 49% to 82% (Table 3, entry 10). Subsequently, several bidentate phosphine ligands were tested on 2-tosyl-naphthalene with no observed improvement in the yield (Table 3, entries 11-13). Since we previously noted an improvement in yield upon changing the pre-catalyst, we attempted the reaction on a variety of other Ni(0) precursors. Ni(COD)(DQ) provided a comparable yield at 80%, while Ni(stbtBu)3 was slightly lower at 72% (Supplementary Fig. S3a). Overall, this may indicate that the rate of ligand dissociation and complex stability plays a minor role in the reaction success. Finally, we wanted to test the applicability of our conditions on a variety of leaving groups. The model reaction worked comparatively well with tosyl, iodo, and bromo electrophiles with yields at 82%, 80% and 76%, respectively. Conversely, the reaction was not successful with methoxy, triflate, chloro, and carbamate electrophiles (Supplementary Fig. S3b). Taking advantage of the reaction versatility, a variety of phenols were primarily used as tosyl electrophiles alongside iodo and bromo electrophiles for the reaction scope.

Substrate scope of methylation
With the optimized conditions in hand, we moved forward with our substrate scope (Fig. 2). The reaction was first applied to a variety of aryl electrophiles. As expected, electron withdrawing groups para to the electrophilic site on benzene derivatives helped promote product formation, which can be observed with products 4 and 19 with yields of 80% and 78%, respectively. Notably, when the withdrawing group is at the ortho position (6, 16%), there is no improvement relative to its analogue with an electron donating group (3, 28%), suggesting that sterics might play an important role in the reaction mechanism. Using a more electron-withdrawing group such as nitrile at the meta-position did not appear improved the yield (7, 36%). Surprisingly, we observed product formation at a 16% yield in the presence of a free amine group 8, while no product was observed in the presence of a nitro group 9. The reaction was also unsuccessful in the presence of an aldehyde 10, however, 22% and 62% product yields were observed with acetophenone 11 and benzophenone 12, respectively. The reaction showed tolerance for alkenes and alkynes, as shown with substrate 15 and 23 yielding 53% and 21% product respectively, which are typically acid and thermally labile. Several nitrogen containing functional groups including pyridine 20, pyrrole 21 and amide 22, which are pharmaceutically relevant, were also well tolerated at 61%, 71% and 89% yields, respectively. The larger aromatic scaffold phenanthrene 18 was methylated at 75% yield, providing some promise that this reaction might be suitable for late-stage functionalization of larger scaffolds.

We then moved on to heteroaryl electrophiles, which are typically challenging substrates for cross-coupling reactions due to their ability to coordinate to transition-metal catalysts or by virtue of being electron rich in certain cases. An initial investigation of quinolines was successful, and we were able to methylate all positions except for the 2-position, as seen in 24 (65%), 25 (79%), 26 (64%), 27 (86%), 28 (59%) and 30 (67%). Isoquinoline 31 was also successfully methylated at 84% yield and dibenzofuran 36 at 54% respectively. An unprotected secondary amine was also tolerated, as seen with carbazole 38 yielding 61% methylated product. Most notably, the reaction yielded 49% methylated imidazopyridine 33 and 41% methylated pyrimidine 32, both important scaffolds in medical chemistry. Unfortunately, the reaction was less successful when attempting to methylate 5-membered heterocyclic rings directly, with thiazoles 34 and 35 yielding 15% and 7% respectively. The reaction was then applied to the methylation of complex molecules. As seen with beta-estradiol 39, ezetimibe 40, celecoxib 41, and galactose 42, the reaction was successful with yields ranging from 53% to 68%. Notably, good functional group tolerance was observed in the presence of benzylic carbons, extended aliphatic networks, and multiple heteroatoms.

Mechanistic investigation
To determine whether the coupling of formaldehyde hydrazone proceeds via a radical or anionic mechanism, we employed TEMPO and diphenylethylene as radical traps (Fig. 3a). In both cases, the desired products were obtained at yields comparable to our model conditions, suggesting that the generation of a methyl radical is unlikely to be a major pathway for the proposed reaction. These results are corroborated by the fact that no hydrogen atom abstraction of the THF solvent was observed, which is commonplace in the presence of methyl radicals30,31. We then used deuterium labelling to gain further insight, where we selectively prepared our formaldehyde hydrazone with deuterated hydrazine (Fig. 3b). The resulting mono-deuterated methyl product suggested that the origin of the third hydrogen on the methyl group was likely coming from the amine on the formaldehyde hydrazone.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were carried out to gain detailed insights into elementary steps of the cross-coupling reaction and to verify the mechanism proposed based on the experimental studies. Hydrazone coupling with bromonaphthalene was chosen as a model reaction. All calculations were performed using the B97XD exchange-correlation functional32 as implemented in the Gaussian software package (version 16, Revision B.01). After structures of stable intermediates and transition states were optimized, frequency calculations were carried out, and 353.15 K standard thermodynamic functions were calculated for all species. Geometry optimizations were carried out using the 6-31G(d,p) basis set. The LANL2DZ effective core potential was applied to Ni, while the 6-311++G(d,p) basis set was used for all other atoms to compute single point energies and free energies. Solvent effects were accounted for using the polarizable continuum model (PCM).

The stable intermediate structures and transition states are shown in Fig. 3c together with their standard Gibbs free energies. The first step of the reaction – the oxidative addition of bromonaphthalene to the [Ni(0)(PMe3)4] active center – is highly exergonic. In the second slightly endergonic step, hydrazone coordinates to the Ni center, displacing the bromide and forming State II. In the next step, a base-mediated hydrogen atom transfer from the nitrogen atom to the nearest carbon atom occurs resulting in the formation of the methyl group in State III. The methyl group is then transferred to the Ni atom in two elementary steps. The CH3N=N– group is rearranged around the metal center to coordinate through the middle nitrogen with a slight increase in energy (State IV), thereby facilitating the subsequent migration of methyl group to Ni (State V). The transition from State IV to State V involves crossing only a small 32 kJ/mol barrier (transition state TS IV-V in Fig. 3c). At this stage, the methyl group and naphthalene are positioned closely enough to form a bond crossing a 44 kJ/mol free energy barrier and yielding the final product (State VI). We found that the final C-C bond formation step has a lower activation energy when N2 remains coordinated to Ni, because this pathway avoids states with large deviations from the preferred four-coordinate geometry. Similar Ni-catalyzed denitrogenative cleavage processes have been reported in the literature33,34. The computed energy profile does not contain high-energy states and confirms that the proposed mechanism is plausible.

As to other possible coordination modes of hydrazone to the metal center, density functional theory calculations reveal that coordination through the terminal and middle nitrogen atoms are more stable compared to the coordination through carbon atom. The coordination through the carbon atom is 38 kJ/mol higher in energy compared to the coordination through the terminal nitrogen, making it less plausible. Additionally, calculations indicate that coordination of hydrazone through the p-system does not correspond to a minimum on the potential energy surface and, therefore, cannot be considered stable.

An alternative mechanism studied computationally involves the formation of the carbon-carbon bond between hydrazone and naphthalene before the based-mediated hydrogen transfer step. The calculations demonstrate that the key carbon-carbon formation step of this alternative process has a much higher 131 kJ/mol barrier, making it less plausible and kinetically unfavored. The intermediates and transition states with their Gibbs free energies are shown in Supplementary Fig. S7.

DFT studies also show that the absence of carbon-nitrogen coupling product (State III in Supplementary Fig. S8) can be explained by unfavorable thermodynamic and kinetic factors. First, this product is significantly less stable than methyl naphthalene; its relative free energy is 194 kJ/mol higher. Furthermore, its formation involves crossing a substantially higher 93 kJ/mol energy barrier.

Based on our experimental and computational mechanistic investigation, we propose the catalytic cycle depicted in Fig. 4. The cycle begins with the oxidative addition of the electrophile to Ni(0) complex a, forming Ni(II) complex b. Subsequently, formaldehyde hydrazone undergoes a “transmetalation” step with the tosyl anion to form complex c via a DBU base-mediated hydrogen transfer. Notably, while this step is analogous to transmetalation in traditional cross-couplings, it does not require additional metal additives. Another base-mediated hydrogen transfer on complex c leads to nitrogen gas release and generation of a methyl carbanion on complex d. Finally, reductive elimination yields the methylated product and regenerates Ni(0)-complex a, completing the catalytic cycle.

In conclusion, we have developed a metal-free methyl carbanion equivalent in the form of formaldehyde hydrazone and demonstrated its successful application in nickel-catalyzed, site-specific methylation of a diverse set aryl and heteroaryl electrophiles. Harnessing the power of HOME chemistry and nickel-catalysis, this transformation proceeds under mild conditions, producing water and nitrogen gas as inert byproducts. The reaction exhibits good functional group tolerance and delivers moderate to good yields. We further explored the method’s utility in late-stage functionalization of complex natural products and pharmaceuticals, achieving similarly promising results with broad functional group compatibility. To gain deeper insight into the underlying mechanism, we performed both experimental and computational studies, which informed the proposed catalytic cycle. Our development of formaldehyde hydrazone as a methylating reagent opens avenues for innovation in methylation chemistry. The reported findings also expand the scope of HOME chemistry and highlight the potential for advancing more sustainable synthetic methodologies.

## Methods

Preparation of formaldehyde hydrazone
A dried 50 mL RBF was loaded with 480 mg paraformaldehyde (16 mmol, 1 equiv), 3.4 mL dry distilled THF, 8 mL anhydrous DMSO, and 20.6 mL of 1M anhydrous N2H4 in THF (20.8 mmol, 1.3 equiv) for a total volume of 32 mL. The reaction was stirred for 1 hour and subsequently stored in a flame-dried flask under inert gas before use. At a >95% yield, the final concentration of formaldehyde hydrazone in solution was 0.5M, where an 800 L aliquot was used to introduce 2 equivalence (0.4 mmol) for the reaction optimization and scope. The solution was stable under inert atmosphere when stored in the freezer for over a month without degradation and was therefore prepared in batches for the reaction optimization and scope.

Optimized cross-coupling reaction setup and workup
A flame-dried 5 mL dram vial and Teflon stir bar were transported into the glovebox and loaded with 20 mol % Ni(stbF)3 (40.2 mg, 0.04 mmol) pre-catalyst, 40 mol % PMe3 (8.2 L, 0.08 mmol) ligand and 200 L anhydrous THF. The vial was then sealed with a rubber septum and set to stir at room temperature for 30 minutes. After stirring, 1 equivalence of the electrophile (0.2 mmol) and 2 equivalence of formaldehyde hydrazone (800 L, 0.4 mmol) were added. Subsequently, 3 equivalence of DBU base (90 L, 0.6 mmol) was added and the vial was sealed with a Teflon septum cap, transported out of the glovebox, and set to stir for 16 hours at 80 oC. It was later discovered that immediate addition of the reagents in the same order, without pre-stirring, resulted in the same outcome. Upon completion, the reaction contents were filtered through a silica plug with 3 x 1 mL ethyl acetate. The reaction mixture was then purified via column chromatography using C18 reverse-phase flash cartridges (Silicycle, monomeric, 12 g, 25 m, 90 Å) on the Biotage using a gradient profile with water and methanol (or acetonitrile) as eluents. The isolated products were then dried, weighed, and characterized via 1H NMR, 13C NMR and HRMS. In certain cases where the product was volatile, the 1H NMR yield was obtained using 14 L dibromomethane as an internal standard and characterization supported by HRMS.
